title: Christmas Pudding
subtitle: The classic British steamed fruit pudding
excerpt: A rich, dark steamed pudding packed with dried fruit, suet, breadcrumbs, and warming spice, made weeks ahead and steamed again on Christmas Day. Turned out and flamed with brandy at the table.

recipe.sourceNotes: Christmas pudding, also called plum pudding (in which plum historically meant any dried fruit), has its origins in medieval pottages made from spiced, sweetened meat and dried fruit. The modern boiled or steamed version developed in the seventeenth century, and by the Victorian era had become the centrepiece of the British Christmas table. Prince Albert's German Christmas traditions reinforced the dish's place in the national repertoire. The tradition of making the pudding on Stir-up Sunday (the last Sunday before Advent) allows the pudding to mature and deepen in flavour over the weeks before Christmas. The coins or charms historically stirred into the mixture are edible good-luck talismans. Brandy butter is the canonical accompaniment, though brandy cream and custard are also served.

recipeTools.notes: A large saucepan deep enough to hold the pudding basin on a trivet.

content.text: Make the pudding at least three weeks before Christmas; six to eight weeks is better. The long rest allows the alcohol to permeate the fruit and the flavours to meld and deepen. On Christmas Day, steam again for 2 hours to heat through completely. Top up the steaming water carefully so it never runs dry.
The night before: combine the mixed dried fruit, currants, mixed peel, and brandy in a large bowl. Stir, cover, and leave overnight to macerate.

Next day: add all the remaining ingredients to the fruit and stir thoroughly. Everyone in the household traditionally takes a stir and makes a wish. The mixture should be a thick, spoonable consistency. Spoon into a buttered 1.2-litre pudding basin. Cover with pleated greaseproof paper and foil. Tie securely.

Place on a trivet in a large saucepan. Add boiling water to come halfway up the sides. Steam over steady medium-low heat for 6 hours, topping up with boiling water every hour. Cool completely, then replace the covering with fresh paper and store in a cool, dark place for at least 3 weeks. Feed with a tablespoon of brandy weekly if wished.

On Christmas Day: steam the pudding again for 2 hours. Turn out onto a warm plate. To flame: heat 3 tablespoons of brandy in a small saucepan until just warm, pour over the pudding, and light immediately. Serve with brandy butter or custard.
